answer:
ARGUMENT

**Temporal Proximity Alone Does Not Establish Causation Unless the Timing Is Unusually Suggestive.**

A retaliation plaintiff must prove a causal connection between protected activity and an adverse employment action. Sequence is not causation. To establish the causal link at the prima facie stage, a plaintiff ordinarily must show either an unusually suggestive proximity in time between the protected activity and the allegedly retaliatory action, or a pattern of antagonism combined with timing. *Lauren W. ex rel. Jean W. v. DeFlaminis*, 480 F.3d 259, 267 (3d Cir. 2007). Timing by itself therefore carries the plaintiff's burden only in the exceptional case. This Court has long required that timing be "unusually suggestive" of retaliatory motive before a causal link will be inferred from it. *Krouse v. Am. Sterilizer Co.*, 126 F.3d 494, 503 (3d Cir. 1997).

*Clark County School District v. Breeden*, 532 U.S. 268, 273–74 (2001) (per curiam), points the same way. The Supreme Court observed that cases accepting temporal proximity alone as sufficient evidence of causality for a prima facie case uniformly require that the proximity be "very close." This Court has likewise treated unusually suggestive timing as the circumstance in which proximity may, on its own, support the inference. *See LeBoon v. Lancaster Jewish Cmty. Ctr. Ass'n*, 503 F.3d 217, 232–33 (3d Cir. 2007).

An interval measured in months ordinarily will not meet that standard. A two-month gap between protected activity and adverse action was not unusually suggestive in *Williams v. Philadelphia Housing Authority Police Department*, 380 F.3d 751, 760 (3d Cir. 2004). And this Court has stated that a gap of three months, without more, cannot create an inference of causation and defeat summary judgment. *LeBoon*, 503 F.3d at 233. Although no bright-line rule fixes the point at which proximity becomes unusually suggestive, *id.* at 232–33, the burden to show that it has been reached remains the plaintiff's.

When timing is not unusually suggestive, the plaintiff must come forward with something more. Courts may then examine the intervening period for proof such as actual antagonistic conduct or animus. *Marra v. Phila. Hous. Auth.*, 497 F.3d 286, 302 (3d Cir. 2007). The question becomes whether the proffered evidence, viewed as a whole, suffices to raise the inference. *Daniels v. Sch. Dist. of Phila.*, 776 F.3d 181, 196 (3d Cir. 2015); *LeBoon*, 503 F.3d at 232. That inquiry is flexible, but it is not empty. It requires evidence, not conjecture drawn from the calendar.

Decisions favoring employees are consistent with this rule. *Kachmar v. SunGard Data Systems, Inc.*, 109 F.3d 173, 177–78 (3d Cir. 1997), held that the passage of time is not conclusive proof against retaliation and that other kinds of evidence may establish the causal link. That principle allows a plaintiff to overcome weak timing with other proof; it does not excuse the absence of such proof. Likewise, *Farrell v. Planters Lifesavers Co.*, 206 F.3d 271, 279–81 (3d Cir. 2000), reversed summary judgment on a record that paired timing with other evidence suggesting retaliation. *Farrell* thus illustrates that where proximity is not itself unusually suggestive, timing must be considered together with other evidence. *See id.* at 280–81.

Here, [Plaintiff] relies on an interval of [length of interval] between [protected activity] and [adverse action]. That interval is not unusually suggestive. [Plaintiff] identifies no pattern of antagonism, no animus during the intervening period, and no other evidence that, viewed with the timing, would permit a reasonable factfinder to infer that retaliation caused [adverse action]. Because chronology is all [Plaintiff] offers, causation fails, and with it the retaliation claim. This Court should affirm the judgment in favor of [Employer].
